source.title: When Refusal Looks Safe: The Refusal-Cue Shortcut in Safety Guard Models
source.authors: Yu Feng; Chun-Ting Zang; Chen Shen; Rui Miao; Ge Teng; Wei-Dong Cai; Jie-Ping Ye

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or missing central sections; the text includes the main paper and appendix.
record.tranche_reason: Extends the refusal-related question to response-level safety guard classifiers and tests whether cue-induced harmfulness flips and explicit refusal decisions are functionally separable. It does not test the original residual-stream direction in chat models.
record.gate_note: The study measures harmfulness and explicit-refusal output flips in safety guards after inserting refusal cues, and tests component suppression. It does not measure a difference-in-means residual direction. The paper also reports training-data label counts, cue formulations, and other results that do not directly measure the tested separability claim; these are not cataloged as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests response-level safety-guard classifiers, not the refusal behaviour of chat models. Its 'refusal' measure is the guard labelling a third-party response as a refusal. That is refusal recognition, not the model deciding to refuse. Its 'harmfulness' measure is the guard's verdict on a response, not an internal harm representation that drives the model's own refusal. It finds, projects out or adds no difference-in-means direction, and does not measure refusal arising in a generative model. Arditi et al. and Zhao et al. appear only in related work. The record's V5 link mixes up refusal recognition by a classifier with the model's refusal decision. The separability finding belongs under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that safety guards learn a refusal-cue shortcut from imbalanced training data, so inserted refusal text flips harmful verdicts. The shortcut is widespread, persists across positions, and is stronger in smaller variants. Sparse component suppression cuts cue-induced failures by about 79-80% while preserving clean harmfulness and refusal-recognition performance. They read this as evidence that shortcut reliance and refusal recognition are partially separable.
record.recipe_differences: The study inserts natural-language refusal cues into safety-guard responses and suppresses associated attention heads and MLP neurons. It neither computes nor intervenes on a harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream direction in a generative chat model.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by guard model and cue; the study reports differing harmfulness/refusal flip coupling and residual cue-induced refusal flips after masking.

fits_no_version.finding: In five safety-guard classifiers, refusal-cue-induced harmful-to-unharmful flips co-occur with refusal-label flips only partially: Pr(FR|FH) ranges from 18.6% to 65.5%. Sparse masking of 0.7-8.6% of heads and neurons cuts RFR@3 from a mean of 25.27% to 7.66%, with refusal F1 changing by at most 2.11 points.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In response-level safety guards, the refusal-cue shortcut in harmfulness classification is partially separable, at the component level, from recognition of genuine refusals.

record.problems: The results concern response-level safety guards rather than generative chat models or a residual-stream refusal direction. The paper reports no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the cataloged rates. The flattened Table 3 text omits model labels, so its model mapping relies on the stated order of eligible guards.
record.rows_left_out: No additional V5-relevant rows were omitted. Other paper results include training-data audits, cue-strength comparisons, model-family vulnerability rates, and harmfulness mitigation metrics, which do not directly measure separability between harmfulness and explicit refusal decisions.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction, ablation or addition; no chat-model refusal.
No abliteration weight edit of a refusal direction.
No jailbreak analysis or training against ablation.
No measure of a chat model's harm representation vs its own refusal decision; guards only label third-party responses.
No transfer across languages, variants or base/instruct.
Training-data effects concern guard shortcut vulnerability, not formation of a refusal direction.

record.verdict_notes: The Table 3 model order (WG-7B, GR-1B, GR-8B, QG-0.6B, QG-8B) is present in the flattened text and the prose confirms the values (e.g. WG-7B RFR@3 51.52, QG-8B Pr(FR|FH) 18.6), so the record's subject mapping is right. The masking rows are the authors' own mitigation method's performance. The study concerns classifiers, not the refusal direction in chat models.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means residual direction is found, projected out, or added; no chat-model refusal behavior or general capability test.
No abliteration-style weight edit of a refusal direction in released chat models. The study suppresses guard components associated with a textual refusal-cue shortcut.
No jailbreak attack or training against ablation is evaluated.
No affine, cone, or multiple-direction account of a generative model’s refusal direction is tested.
Tests output-level functional separability in safety guards, not the geometry or representation of harmfulness and refusal in safety-trained chat models.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer of a refusal direction.
Compares guards with different data characteristics but does not vary refusal training to test whether or when a removable direction forms.
No reasoning chat models or reasoning-before-answer refusal direction are tested.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Explicit-refusal safety guards on WildGuardTest with head-position insertion of three primary refusal cues
reader_labels.reason: The flips are positively associated but only partially coupled: Pr(FR | FH) ranges from 18.6% to 65.5%, and component suppression reduces rather than eliminates cue-induced refusal flips while clean refusal measures change modestly (r1-r40).
